title: Turn to modern jazz via Alton Purnell, Alden Ashforth and Lawrence's bitterness
summary: Passing chords, Alden Ashforth's records and guitar influences led him from traditional to modern jazz; Lawrence's disillusion with the Lewis band pushed him the same way; he argues jazz must compose for the present.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Sure. Yeah, just talk. Just say anything that comes to your mind. No, I'd rather not do that. . .

Well, uh, when I was about fifteen, uh, uh, actually through the efforts of Alvin Purnell. You see, I used to sit in with George Lewis and Alvin Purnell had a thing going where he'd play passing chords. And, uh, I was told when I was a kid that I had some kind of fantastic gear. I was some kind of child prodigy or something, you see. And so, uh, I'd hear all the things he was playing. And I'd tell Lawrence, why aren't you playing the same chords Alton's playing? You know, they sound like they're fitting more into the harmonic context of what's going on, you know? I'd notice that George would play a G seventh chord, run a G seventh chord against a D seventh chord. And this was sort of an unconscious dissonance. So I began to hear all these things. And, uh, through, basically throughout him, you know, I began to, uh, realize, uh, this concept of passing chords and such. And I began to get interested in modern jazz. And, uh, I had stopped listening to classics, except, uh, with the exception of, of light opera. And, and my dad, uh, would take us to, uh, different shows that were coming down, stage shows, musical comedies. And, uh, so all this kind of amalgamation of things, I guess, kind of pushed me into modern jazz. I became interested in, uh, I should say really that the, the, uh, turning point was, uh, when I met, uh, Alden Ashforth. And came down from the Wall Islands and we had known Dizzy and Charlie Parker and his people. And I began to listen to the records that he had. And I began to switch to guitar. And at first I played tenor guitar. And, uh, uh, really I began to listen, well, I had, when I was playing banjo, I had listened a lot to Lonnie Johnson. And, uh, Eddie Lang. And then Freddie Green. It was a very natural development, you know. Then I began to listen to, to, uh, I guess Teddy Wilson and Coleman Hawkins and people of that sort. And Benny Goodman. And Christian. Christian, Christian sense of time. Then I began to realize that the, the same sense of time that, that, that guys like Bunke played with, you know, that, that same time feeling was this, actually it was the same time feeling that the modernists were playing with. But it was only, uh, only using different technical aspects of the instruments. But actually the same Negro-ed feeling, you know, was, was, uh, was there. I found it very easy to make the transition rhythmically. And actually it was a liberation in, in, in a lot of ways for me, because I'd been hearing so many things that I couldn't apply to traditional jazz. And I began to play modern jazz. I think Lawrence too instilled in me a, a lot of things that, that, uh, that, uh, brought me around to modern jazz. Uh, Lawrence was pretty disgusted with the George Lewis band in general. And he used to say that all the, all the, all the, at least 90% of the musicians around town were only trying to do things that had been done long before. And he was quite bitter about these things and his attitude towards, towards, uh, traditional jazz. This was not, this was an unconscious thing on this part. He wasn't trying to turn me away from the Warriors jazz, but he was just talking about these things and naturally they turned me away. Uh, he was quite bitter about the whole thing. And he felt he wasn't much of a musician himself. He felt that his brother had been the musician of the family, his brother and his father, Billy. And, uh, through his efforts, I think, uh, I began to see that, that possibly this music, although valid at its time, was, was, uh, losing this validity. You see. Although I realized that if something is, is truly, is truly art, that it survives. And I think this is something that all jazz musicians should realize. And I think that if jazz is to endure, this should be realized. However, I think that you do have to compose for, for the present. If you are a genuine artist, if you do feel art genuine, that you have to compose for the present. Whether you're playing jazz, whether you're composing classics, no matter what you're doing, you have to work for the present. So basically that's about, that's about what my development has been.
